title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
scopeHtml: Scope: headers, methods, caching headers, cookies, CORS, keep-alive, head-of-line blocking across versions. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: HTTP basics: requests, responses, methods
notes.html:
HTTP is a request/response protocol: the client sends a method, a path, headers and an optional body; the server replies with a status code, headers and a body. It is stateless: each request stands alone.

GET /orders/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.shop.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 58
Method Meaning Safe Idempotent
GET Read yes yes
HEAD Headers only yes yes
POST Create/action no no
PUT Replace no yes
PATCH Partial update no not guaranteed
DELETE Remove no yes
OPTIONS What is allowed (CORS preflight) yes yes

Status families. 2xx ok (200, 201, 204), 3xx redirect (301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 not modified), 4xx client error (400, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404, 409 conflict, 429 rate limit), 5xx server (500, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 gateway timeout).

Worked example. Idempotency matters for retries. A mobile app times out on POST /payments. Retrying may charge twice. Stripe solves it with an Idempotency-Key header: the server stores the first result for that key (24 h) and returns it for repeats. PUT /users/7 can be retried blindly.

Industry examples. REST APIs at Stripe, GitHub and Twilio follow these methods and use 429 plus Retry-After. 502 vs 504 is the daily vocabulary of ops: 502 means the proxy got garbage or a closed connection, 504 means it waited too long.

Everyday analogy. Posting a letter and getting a reply: the method is what you ask ("tell me", "store this"), the status is the first line of the answer ("done", "not here", "we messed up").

Common interview traps.

  • Calling POST idempotent, or using GET for actions that change state (crawlers and prefetch will trigger them).
  • Confusing 401 (who are you?) with 403 (I know you, no).
  • Returning 200 with an error in the body; breaks caches, monitors and retries.

notes.title: HTTP/1.1: keep-alive and its limits
notes.html:
HTTP/1.1 reuses one TCP connection for many requests (keep-alive, default since 1.1), but responses must come back in order on that connection.

Without keep-alive every request pays TCP handshake (1 RTT) plus TLS (1 to 2 RTT). With a 100 ms RTT that is 200 to 300 ms before the first byte. Keep-alive removes that for later requests.

The limit is head-of-line (HOL) blocking at the HTTP level: request 2 cannot be answered until response 1 is finished. Pipelining (sending several without waiting) existed but was broken in practice and is disabled in browsers. Workarounds browsers used: open 6 parallel connections per host, and sites used domain sharding, sprite sheets and bundling to cut requests.

Worked example. A page needs 60 assets. With 6 connections and 100 ms per request round, the minimum is 60/6 x 100 ms = 1 s of pure waiting, even on a fast link. Bundling to 10 files cuts it to about 200 ms.

Config (nginx).

# nginx.conf (keepalive to clients and upstreams)
keepalive_timeout 65;
keepalive_requests 1000;
upstream api { server 10.0.0.5:8080; keepalive 64; }
# proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection "";

Industry examples. HTTP/1.1 is still what many internal services and simple clients speak. A slow upstream behind a proxy with keepalive off causes connection churn (TIME_WAIT pile-ups, ephemeral port exhaustion).

Everyday analogy. A single-lane drive-through: you can keep the lane open for many cars, but a slow order delays everyone behind it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying pipelining solves HOL blocking in 1.1 (it does not, in practice).
  • Forgetting that keepalive timeouts must be longer on the client side than on the server, or a race closes a connection mid-request (classic sporadic 502 behind AWS ALB when the app idle timeout is shorter than the ALB's 60 s).

notes.title: HTTP/2: multiplexing
notes.html:
HTTP/2 sends many requests as interleaved binary frames over ONE TCP connection, so a slow response no longer blocks others at the HTTP layer.

Key features:

  • Streams and frames: each request/response is a numbered stream; frames from different streams interleave.
  • HPACK header compression: repeated headers (cookies, user-agent) cost a few bytes after the first request. Saves 80 to 90% of header bytes.
  • Stream prioritization and flow control per stream and per connection.
  • Server push: sent assets before asked. Largely abandoned; Chrome removed it.
  • Usually requires TLS in browsers (ALPN negotiates h2).
Stream 1: HEADERS(GET /a) ....... DATA DATA
Stream 3: HEADERS(GET /b) .. DATA ..... DATA
Stream 5: HEADERS(GET /c) DATA
(all in one TCP connection, interleaved)

Worked example. The 60-asset page: one connection, all 60 requests started at once. Time is about 1 RTT plus transfer time instead of 10 sequential rounds. Bundling and sharding become anti-patterns (sharding even hurts, since it kills multiplexing).

The catch: TCP HOL blocking. All streams share one TCP byte stream. If one packet is lost, TCP holds back everything after it until retransmit. On lossy mobile networks (2% loss) HTTP/2 can be slower than six HTTP/1.1 connections.

Industry examples. gRPC runs on HTTP/2. Nginx, Envoy, Cloudflare, AWS ALB all speak it. Google created SPDY, the ancestor.

Decision gravity. Enabling h2 at the edge is reversible and safe (clients fall back). Keep h2 for client-to-edge, and consider HTTP/1.1 or h2 to origin depending on proxy support.

Everyday analogy. A single conveyor belt carrying mixed packages for many customers, rather than one belt per customer. If the belt jams, every customer waits.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing HTTP/2 removes all head-of-line blocking; TCP-level HOL remains.
  • Claiming h2 is faster for one big file; it is not.
  • Forgetting max concurrent streams (often 100 to 128) and HTTP/2 rapid reset attacks (2023), which led to server hardening.

notes.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC
notes.html:
HTTP/3 runs HTTP over QUIC, a transport built on UDP, so lost packets only stall the one stream they belong to.

QUIC features:

  • Per-stream loss recovery: removes TCP HOL blocking.
  • TLS 1.3 built in: handshake in 1 RTT, and 0-RTT for repeat visits (replayable, so only for safe requests).
  • Connection IDs: a connection survives a switch from Wi-Fi to cellular (connection migration), because it is not tied to the IP/port 4-tuple.
  • User-space implementation: easier to evolve than kernel TCP; but more CPU.
  • Discovered by the Alt-Svc: h3=":443" header or HTTPS DNS record; browsers fall back to h2 if UDP 443 is blocked.

Worked example. RTT 80 ms to a mobile user. HTTP/2 with TLS 1.3: 1 RTT TCP + 1 RTT TLS + 1 request = ~240 ms to first byte. HTTP/3: 1 RTT handshake + request = ~160 ms; with 0-RTT resumption ~80 ms.

Industry examples. Google, YouTube, Facebook, Cloudflare and Netflix use HTTP/3; roughly a quarter to a third of web traffic by 2024. Corporate firewalls that drop UDP are the main blocker.

Decision gravity. Enabling h3 at a CDN is a toggle (reversible). Self-hosting needs UDP load balancing (QUIC connection-ID-aware, e.g. Katran) and watching CPU, a bigger commitment.

Everyday analogy. Separate lanes in a motorway that do not stop when one lane has a crash, and a car that keeps its toll tag even when it takes a different road.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying QUIC is "UDP so unreliable". Reliability is implemented in QUIC.
  • Forgetting UDP may be blocked or rate-limited: always keep h2 fallback.
  • 0-RTT replay risk for non-idempotent requests.

notes.title: Headers that matter
notes.html:
Headers are key-value metadata. The ones used in nearly every incident:

  • Host: which site on this IP (required in 1.1; :authority in h2/h3).
  • Content-Type / Accept / Content-Length / Transfer-Encoding: chunked: body description. Request smuggling arises when proxies disagree about Content-Length vs chunked.
  • Authorization: Bearer <token> or Basic.
  • User-Agent, Accept-Encoding (gzip, br), Content-Encoding: compression cuts JSON by 70 to 90%.
  • X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, Forwarded: the real client IP and scheme once a proxy is in the path. Trust only the proxy-appended last hop.
  • Location: redirect target.
  • Retry-After: how long to wait on 429/503.
  • Connection / Upgrade: protocol switch (WebSocket).
  • Cache-Control, ETag, Vary: next section.

Tool sample.

$ curl -sI https://api.shop.com/orders/42
HTTP/2 200
content-type: application/json
cache-control: private, max-age=0
etag: "a1b2c3"
content-encoding: br
x-request-id: 7f3e...

Worked example. A 200 KB JSON response compresses to ~30 KB with gzip. At 1,000 rps that is 1,000 x 170 KB = 170 MB/s of bandwidth saved, ~1.4 Gbit/s.

Everyday analogy. The labels on a parcel: where from, what is inside, handle with care, return address.

Common interview traps.

  • Trusting X-Forwarded-For from the client for rate limiting or auth: it can be forged.
  • Forgetting Vary: Accept-Encoding (cache serves gzip to a client that cannot read it).
  • Header size limits (8 KB in nginx by default) breaking large cookies with 431/400 errors.

notes.title: Caching headers
notes.html:
HTTP caching lets browsers, CDNs and proxies reuse a response instead of asking the origin again. Two mechanisms: freshness (do not even ask) and validation (ask cheaply "has it changed?").

  • Cache-Control: max-age=3600 (browser), s-maxage=86400 (shared caches such as CDN), public, private (browser only), no-store (never keep), no-cache (keep but revalidate), immutable, stale-while-revalidate=60.
  • Validators: ETag: "v7" with request If-None-Match: "v7"; or Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since. If unchanged, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body.
  • Vary: which request headers change the response (e.g. Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language).
1st:  GET /app.js            -> 200, ETag "v7", max-age=60, 300 KB
2nd (after 60 s):
      GET /app.js If-None-Match "v7" -> 304, 0 KB body

Worked example (best practice). Fingerprinted assets app.4f9a2c.js: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. HTML: Cache-Control: no-cache so it always revalidates but is cheap via ETag. API with user data: private, no-store. A CDN hit ratio of 95% on 10,000 rps means the origin sees 500 rps instead of 10,000.

Industry examples. Cloudflare, Fastly and CloudFront honour s-maxage; GitHub serves releases with long cache and ETags. Fastly pioneered fast purge.

Decision gravity. A long max-age on a non-fingerprinted URL is nearly a one-way door: you cannot recall copies in users' browsers. Prefer versioned URLs.

Everyday analogy. Keeping yesterday's newspaper: still fresh if the news cannot have changed; otherwise phone the paper and ask "anything new?"; they say "no" in two words (304).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing no-cache (revalidate) with no-store (do not store).
  • Caching personalised responses publicly (a classic data leak: one user's page served to another).
  • Forgetting Vary or cookies, so the CDN fragment cache explodes or leaks.

notes.title: Cookies and sessions
notes.html:
A cookie is a small value the server asks the browser to store and send back on every request to that site. It is how a stateless protocol gets "login".

Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; Path=/; Max-Age=1800; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

  • Secure: only over HTTPS.
  • HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read it (blunts XSS theft).
  • SameSite: Strict, Lax (default in modern browsers), None (needs Secure) controls sending on cross-site requests (CSRF defence).
  • Domain/Path/Max-Age/Expires: scope and lifetime.
  • Limit about 4 KB each, ~50 per domain; sent with every request, so large cookies waste bandwidth (and defeat CDN caching).
  • __Host- prefix forces Secure, no Domain, Path=/.

Worked example. A 2 KB cookie on 40 requests per page load = 80 KB upstream per page, on a slow mobile uplink (1 Mbit/s) about 0.6 s. Serve static assets from a cookieless domain, or keep the cookie small and put data in the server-side session store.

Industry examples. Chrome phasing out third-party cookies and defaulting to SameSite=Lax changed how embedded widgets, SSO and ad tech work. Mobile apps typically use bearer tokens instead.

Everyday analogy. A wristband at a concert: shown at every gate, and it says which ticket you hold, not who you are.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing the session data in the cookie unsigned.
  • Missing Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite on auth cookies.
  • Forgetting cookies are per-domain and the sub-domain (Domain=) scoping rules.

notes.title: CORS
notes.html:
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the browser's rule that a page from one origin may only read responses from another origin if that server explicitly allows it. An origin is scheme + host + port. It is enforced by browsers, not servers; curl ignores it.

Flow:

  • Simple request (GET, simple POST with basic headers): browser sends it with an Origin header; response must include Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • Preflight: for PUT/DELETE, JSON content type or custom headers (Authorization), browser first sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method/Headers; server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, Access-Control-Max-Age (cache the preflight, e.g. 600).
  • Credentials: cookies cross-origin need Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and a specific origin (not *).

Config (nginx).

# add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin "https://app.shop.com" always;
# add_header Access-Control-Allow-Methods "GET, POST, OPTIONS" always;
# add_header Access-Control-Allow-Headers "Authorization, Content-Type" always;
# add_header Access-Control-Max-Age 600 always;
# add_header Vary Origin always;

Worked example. SPA at app.shop.com calls api.shop.com with an Authorization header: each call is two requests (OPTIONS + GET). With Max-Age: 600 the preflight is cached 10 minutes, cutting API traffic by ~half.

Industry examples. Public APIs like GitHub's allow * for unauthenticated reads. Many "CORS errors" in the console are really a 500/502 that lacks CORS headers, hiding the real error.

Everyday analogy. A building where residents may only read mail from another floor if that floor's concierge has pre-approved them.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking CORS is server-side security. It protects users' browsers, not your API.
  • Allow-Origin: * with credentials is rejected.
  • Reflecting any Origin header back: effectively disables the protection. Also forgetting Vary: Origin when allow-listing.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• HTTP is stateless request/response: methods (safe/idempotent), status families, headers; use idempotency keys for payments.
  • HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses a connection but suffers HTTP-level head-of-line blocking; browsers open about 6 connections.
  • HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection with HPACK; TCP-level HOL blocking remains on loss.
  • HTTP/3 over QUIC (UDP) fixes that, has 1-RTT/0-RTT setup and connection migration; keep h2 fallback.
  • Caching: Cache-Control, ETag/304, Vary; fingerprint static assets and give them a year, never cache private data publicly.
  • Cookies need Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite; keep them small.
  • CORS is a browser rule enforced via Origin and preflight OPTIONS; cache preflights; never reflect arbitrary origins.
